text: Combine the last two lessons' codes correctly, and you get something neither one alone could do: protection against an arbitrary single-qubit error. This was the first proof, in 1995, that quantum error correction was possible at all.

The bit-flip code fixes any single X error but is blind to Z. The phase-flip code fixes any single Z error but is blind to X. Shor's insight was to concatenate them: use the phase-flip code as an outer code, and protect each of its 3 qubits using the bit-flip code as an inner code. Since the outer code has 3 blocks, and each block's qubit is replaced by 3 physical qubits of an inner code, the total count is 3 times 3, or 9 physical qubits, protecting 1 logical qubit.

Any single-qubit error reduces to X, Z, or both together as Y. The concatenated structure handles all three: an X error on one of the 9 qubits is caught by the inner bit-flip code covering that qubit's block, before it can affect the outer layer at all. A Z error on any qubit within a block flips that whole block's overall phase the same way regardless of which inner qubit it hits, so the outer phase-flip code catches it at the block level. And a Y error gets its X part fixed by the inner code and its Z part fixed by the outer code, independently and simultaneously. This was the historic result: a single code, built from two codes that each only handled half the problem, correcting any single-qubit Pauli error on any one of its 9 physical qubits — the first concrete proof that no-cloning and the continuous nature of quantum errors don't actually prevent error correction from working.

But 9 qubits per logical qubit, while modest-sounding, caps out at exactly 1 correctable error. Scaling up to handle more simultaneous errors means more levels of concatenation, which grows the physical-qubit cost exponentially, and the code doesn't match the local, nearest-neighbor connectivity real superconducting or trapped-ion hardware has. The Shor code's importance is historical and pedagogical — it proved the concept, but it isn't what a real fault-tolerance roadmap uses today.
Next lesson builds the actual circuit behind every syndrome table you've seen so far — the mechanism that lets you learn what error happened without ever learning what the data is.
